```{r setup, include=FALSE}
  fig.height = 4.5, dpi = 120, out.width = "100%", raster3d = 1e5, dev = "svglite", fig.ext = "svg",
  dev.args = list(pointsize = 14))
PAL <- c(blue = "#2E6F9E", red = "#B5342B", green = "#3F7A3D",
         orange = "#9E5E0F", purple = "#7A4F9E", teal = "#2A7A7A",
         grey = "#5C6166")
library(ggplot2)
library(ggplot3d)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 17) + theme(
  plot.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA),
  panel.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA),
  legend.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA),
  legend.key = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA),
  legend.box.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA),
  legend.position = "none"))
```

Ray marching evaluates a field along each viewing ray to find a surface or
accumulate colour through a volume. This article renders both kinds of field,
combines them with other layers and adds diffuse light transport with the
native path tracer. Installation is covered in [Get started](ggplot3d.html).

## Tracing a distance surface

A signed distance function (SDF) gives negative values inside a shape, zero
on its surface and positive values outside. Build a sphere with a cylindrical
hole by subtracting a capsule, a cylinder with rounded ends. The constructors
and shape algebra are described in [Implicit surfaces](implicit-surfaces.html).

```{r distance-shape}
ball <- sdf_sphere(radius = 0.8)
hole <- sdf_capsule(c(0, -1.2, 0), c(0, 1.2, 0), radius = 0.3)
shape <- ball - hole
```

Set the three scale limits explicitly to bound the field. The trace mode of
`geom_isofunction_3d()` finds the zero surface directly at each raster sample.
Sphere tracing advances by a conservative distance bound, following
Hart [1996](https://doi.org/10.1007/s003710050084).

```{r traced-surface, fig.alt="A blue sphere with a cylindrical hole running through its centre."}
surface <- ggplot() +
  geom_isofunction_3d(fun = shape, render = "trace", fill = PAL["blue"]) +
  xlim(-1, 1) + ylim(-1, 1) + scale_z_continuous(limits = c(-1, 1))
surface + coord_3d(azimuth = -65, elevation = 25,
  backend = backend_3d("raster", dpi = 60, antialias = 1))
```

Trace mode requires an SDF object and an opaque fill. It uses transformed
scale coordinates, the panel clipping box and depth occlusion. Control the
surface residual with `trace_tolerance` and the maximum steps per ray with
`trace_steps`. Mesh mode accepts ordinary R functions and produces triangles
for the model exporters in [Exporting plots and scenes](export.html).

## Integrating a scalar volume

A scalar volume has one value at every combination of x, y and z coordinates.
The complete rectilinear grid can have unequal spacing on its axes; rows are
matched by coordinate. The example below evaluates a smooth field on a
12 by 12 by 12 grid, with a larger concentration left of centre and a smaller
one to its right.

```{r volume-data}
a <- seq(-1, 1, length.out = 12)
field <- expand.grid(x = a, y = a, z = a)
field$value <- with(field,
  exp(-8 * ((x + 0.35)^2 + y^2 + z^2)) +
  0.7 * exp(-14 * ((x - 0.45)^2 + (y - 0.2)^2 + z^2)))
range(field$value)
```

Emission-absorption rendering accumulates colour and extinction along a ray.
The transfer function maps scalar values to colours and extinction
coefficients, following the optical model reviewed by
Max [1995](https://doi.org/10.1109/2945.468400). The opacity ramp below maps the
minimum field value to zero extinction and the maximum to four per transformed
data unit. A constant coefficient of four across a distance of one transmits
`exp(-4)` of the incoming light.

```{r absorption, fig.alt="Two blue concentrations in a translucent volume, with the larger concentration left of centre."}
volume <- ggplot(field, aes(x, y, z = z, value = value))
volume + geom_volume_3d(opacity = c(0, 4),
  colours = c("#DCEAF3", PAL[["blue"]]), samples = 48) +
  coord_3d(backend = backend_3d("raster", dpi = 60, antialias = 1))
```

The renderer interpolates values trilinearly between grid samples and
integrates colour in linear light. Increase `samples` to refine absorption
integration along the volume diagonal. Both colour and opacity can also be
functions of scalar values; each is evaluated into a transfer table before
rendering.

## Maximum intensity

Maximum-intensity projection (MIP) shows the greatest scalar value encountered
along each ray. This helps locate concentrated values through the full
depth of a field. Colour and opacity are evaluated at that maximum.

```{r mip, fig.alt="Maximum-intensity projection showing two concentrations in the scalar field."}
volume + geom_volume_3d(mode = "mip", opacity = 1,
  colours = c("#DCEAF3", PAL[["blue"]])) +
  coord_3d(backend = backend_3d("raster", dpi = 60, antialias = 1))
```

The maximum is found from the stationary points of the interpolated field in
each crossed cell. The absorption sampling count has no effect on this mode.

## A volume isosurface

An isosurface consists of points at a chosen scalar value. Set the level
explicitly to show the boundary around the two concentrations. The first
intersection along each ray supplies the visible surface and its normal.

```{r volume-iso, fig.alt="Two shaded isosurface lobes at scalar value 0.3."}
volume + geom_volume_3d(mode = "iso", level = 0.3,
  colours = c(PAL[["blue"]], PAL[["blue"]])) +
  coord_3d(backend = backend_3d("raster", dpi = 60, antialias = 1))
```

Root finding uses the cubic restriction of the trilinear field within each
cell, including roots between cell endpoints of the same sign. The level
defaults to the midpoint of the scalar range. Use the mesh-producing
`geom_isosurface_3d()` when you need exported triangle geometry.

## Combining image and vector layers

Traced surfaces and volumes share depth with ordinary raster geometry.
Opaque surfaces stop the volume integral. Transparent raster fragments split
the integral at their depths, and overlapping absorption volumes contribute
emission and extinction jointly.

This scene places a small traced sphere inside the volume and sends a red
line through both. Mark the line for raster rendering so every fragment is
composited with the field at its depth.

```{r mixed-raster, fig.alt="A scalar volume containing an orange sphere, crossed by a red line whose middle is occluded."}
line <- data.frame(x = c(-1, 1), y = 0, z = 0)
mixed <- volume + geom_volume_3d(opacity = c(0, 2), samples = 48) +
  geom_isofunction_3d(fun = sdf_sphere(radius = 0.25), data = data.frame(id = 1),
    render = "trace", fill = PAL["orange"], inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  geom_path_3d(aes(x, y, z = z), data = line, inherit.aes = FALSE,
    colour = PAL["red"], linewidth = 1, raster = TRUE)
mixed + coord_3d(backend = backend_3d("raster", dpi = 60, antialias = 1))
```

Vector and hybrid panels place the traced fields as an image. Ordinary vector
primitives are clipped against the depth where that image reaches half its
opacity. This depth gives an occlusion boundary for the vector line. Use
raster rendering for a line that needs continuous attenuation inside a volume.

```{r mixed-vector, fig.alt="A traced volume and orange sphere embedded as an image, with a red vector line clipped by image coverage."}
vector_line <- volume + geom_volume_3d(opacity = c(0, 2), samples = 48) +
  geom_isofunction_3d(fun = sdf_sphere(radius = 0.25), data = data.frame(id = 1),
    render = "trace", fill = PAL["orange"], inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  geom_path_3d(aes(x, y, z = z), data = line, inherit.aes = FALSE,
    colour = PAL["red"], linewidth = 1)
vector_line + coord_3d(backend = backend_3d("vector", dpi = 60,
  antialias = 1))
```

Select hybrid rendering to rasterize marked geometry and keep the remaining
layers as vectors. The same traced image participates in the panel's depth
test. Hidden strokes behind traced surfaces currently support solid hiding;
`hidden = "dashed"` does not produce dashed strokes there.

```{r mixed-hybrid, fig.alt="The same volume and orange sphere in a hybrid panel with a red vector line."}
vector_line + coord_3d(backend = backend_3d("hybrid", dpi = 60,
  antialias = 1))
```

## Diffuse path tracing

Path tracing samples light paths through successive surface interactions.
The native backend adds diffuse interreflection, soft shadows from a distant
disk and thin-lens depth of field. Its light transport follows
Pharr, Jakob and Humphreys [2023](https://pbr-book.org/4ed/Light_Transport_I_Surface_Reflection/Path_Tracing).

Build a sphere resting above a floor. The ambient light supplies a uniform
environment, and the diffuse contribution supplies the distant light.

```{r path-scene}
floor <- expand.grid(x = c(-1, 1), y = c(-1, 1))
floor$z <- -0.65
lit <- ggplot() +
  geom_isofunction_3d(fun = sdf_sphere(radius = 0.55), render = "trace",
    fill = PAL["blue"]) +
  geom_surface_3d(aes(x, y, z = z), data = floor, fill = "grey85") +
  xlim(-1, 1) + ylim(-1, 1) + scale_z_continuous(limits = c(-0.7, 0.7))
tracer <- backend_3d("pathtrace", samples = 8, bounces = 3, seed = 42,
  dpi = 60, antialias = 1, progressive = TRUE, batch_size = 4)
```

Each redraw adds eight samples per pixel to this backend's accumulator.
Reusing the same backend and scene continues the sequence; changing geometry,
camera, lighting or image dimensions resets it. The seed fixes the random
sequence independently of batch size and thread count.

```{r path-eight, fig.alt="A blue sphere above a grey floor, with a soft shadow in an eight-sample path-traced image."}
traced <- lit + coord_3d(backend = tracer, aspect = "data",
  light = light_3d(direction = c(-1, -1, 2), ambient = 0.2, diffuse = 0.8))
traced
```

Draw the same object again to accumulate sixteen samples per pixel. Increase
the sample count for final output; these small images keep the example quick.
For reproducible independent renders, keep the seed fixed and use the default
`progressive = FALSE`.

```{r path-sixteen, fig.alt="The blue sphere and floor after a second eight-sample pass, accumulating sixteen samples per pixel."}
traced
```

Set a positive `aperture` for depth of field, with the focal plane controlled
by `focus` in aspect-scaled model units. Its default focuses on the camera
target. The path tracer accepts meshes and opaque traced SDF surfaces;
scalar volumes require the raster, vector or hybrid backends described above.
